analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal for oil companies to sell gasoline and other fuels at unjust or unreasonable prices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote; it had three Republican sponsors and no further action after November 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced weeks after hurricanes disrupted fuel supplies and gas prices spiked, the bill would make it unlawful for anyone in the petroleum business to sell crude oil, gasoline, diesel fuel, natural gas, or petroleum distillates at an "unjust or unreasonable" price [S2][S3]. The Federal Trade Commission would have 90 days to write rules defining that term, considering past regional prices, the seller's costs, supply disruptions, and unfair advantage-taking [S3]. Enforcement would prioritize companies earning over $500 million a year in refining and fuel profits, with civil fines of up to $11,000 per violation and criminal penalties reaching $100 million for corporations [S3]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy gasoline, diesel, heating fuel, and natural gas would gain a federal backstop against price spikes, especially during emergencies when supply disruptions are used to justify sudden jumps. The bill directs the FTC to focus enforcement on large refining and fuel companies earning over $500 million per year in profits [S3], so the restraint would fall on major firms rather than small retailers. Existing state price-gouging laws would be preserved [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits selling crude oil, gasoline, diesel fuel, natural gas, or petroleum distillates at an unjust or unreasonable price, creating a federal standard against fuel price gouging [S2][S3].

Directs the FTC to judge unreasonable pricing against regional prices over the prior 12 months, the seller's actual costs, supply disruptions, and signs of unfair advantage, so ordinary cost increases would not be treated as violations [S3].

Tells the FTC to prioritize enforcement against petroleum businesses earning more than $500 million per year in refining, sale, exchange, or shipping profits, concentrating penalties on the largest firms [S3].
Preserves state price-gouging laws and adds criminal penalties of up to $100 million for corporations and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and fuel sellers would bear the cost of federal price regulation, civil fines, and potential criminal liability. Economists and the industry would also argue that the risk of penalties for pricing during supply disruptions could discourage investment in refining capacity and inventories, a cost that could eventually show up in supply reliability.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: The core term "unjust or unreasonable price" is undefined in the bill itself; the FTC would have only 90 days to define it, an unusually short timeline for a rule that determines when a business commits a crime [S3].

The civil penalty of up to $11,000 per violation is small relative to the revenues of major oil companies, raising doubts about how much deterrence the civil enforcement path alone would create; the stronger deterrent is the criminal provision [S3].

Price ceilings during supply shortages can discourage sellers from building inventories or shifting fuel to where it is most needed, a standard economic objection to gouging laws that the bill's cost-based safe harbors partially but not fully address [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and visible harm — sharp fuel price spikes after supply disruptions — and builds in sensible reference points (prior regional prices, actual costs) to separate genuine gouging from normal pricing. But it leans on a vague standard that the FTC would have to define in 90 days, and its civil fines are modest. The idea was responsive to a moment of public anger over gas prices; as drafting, it is a starting point rather than a carefully engineered enforcement regime.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank LoBiondo introduced the bill on October 20, 2005, with Reps. Smith of New Jersey and Emerson as cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S3][S4][S5].
On November 4, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 109th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil and gas producers and refiners are better off, because no federal fuel-pricing standard or penalty regime was enacted. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death, since it never became law to restrain price spikes.

for.name: Rep. Frank LoBiondo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill was referred to a subcommittee on November 4, 2005 and received no further action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and there were no roll-call votes, so the partisan shape of any opposition never became part of the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would have made it unlawful for these companies to sell crude oil, gasoline, diesel, and natural gas at prices the FTC deemed unjust or unreasonable, with enforcement priority on refiners earning over $500 million a year and criminal fines up to $100 million [S3]. The bill died in committee, so these firms kept pricing discretion.

They fall under the same pricing prohibition, but enforcement priority targeted companies with over $500 million in annual profits, putting the compliance burden mainly on large firms; smaller retailers would have faced the rules without being the focus [S3].
